title: Setting up a Classroom with Structured Literacy in Mind
author: Holly Price
summary: A veteran teacher reflects at year end on how she is rearranging her classroom to serve structured literacy rather than the balanced-literacy habits and Instagram aesthetics she inherited. She walks through four areas: the sound wall, the classroom library, the small-group area, and desk formations. Her candid examples include a sound wall that decayed into wallpaper because it was moved away from her teaching area, and a library re-sorted from colored dots and reading levels into character and themed bins. She also reorganizes small-group materials by phonics skill, borrowing a magazine-bin system with hand-written labels, and weighs table groups against pairs of desks. The consistent principle is that room setup should be judged by whether it makes instruction easier to deliver, and that functional beats cute.
points: A sound wall only helps if it sits where teaching happens; placed away from the main teaching area, it became decor rather than a tool.
Library organization carried over from balanced literacy (colored dots, levels) can be replaced with character and themed bins without chaos.
Organizing small-group materials by phonics skill rather than guided reading level saves prep and lets teachers pull skill groups on the fly.
Desk formation is treated as an open instructional question, since students needing proximity during dictation may be better served by desks than clipboards on the carpet.
Her guiding test for classroom setup is functionality for instruction over perfect, matching aesthetics.
quotes: Do I still want to have a cute classroom? Sure! Is that the main focus? No, but sometimes I have to bring myself back down to earth and remind myself of that before purchasing that $350 cute carpet.

I’m going off what I’ve seen with my students, many who have been English Language Learners, students with IEPs, and students receiving speech services. Using a sound wall, (now the key is using!) has really helped move the needle as far as reading and spelling for those students.
Unintentionally, the sound wall became more like wall paper or decor versus the teaching tool that I intended it to be.

At first I was worried that my library would turn into chaos without colored dots. Labeling each book in its separate bin was something I just didn’t have time for. To my surprise, students were able to put books back into the correct bins without individual book labels.

As I started making the shift to structured literacy and collecting decodable texts I realized I needed to rethink my small group organization. I either had to prep way ahead of time, or spend precious teaching time hunting things down.
I’m constantly reminding myself to be less perfect/cute and more functional.

I think of those students who needed to be right up close to me during dictation time, or math time, that I moved to the carpet. They would have really benefited from a desk, versus writing on a clipboard.
